title: Coming Home After a Skin Disease
overview: This chapter sets out the ceremonies for welcoming back someone healed of a serious skin disease, and for dealing with spreading mold in a house.

parts.label: Two birds outside the camp (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: The priest goes out to the person living apart and confirms they have healed; the disease named here covered various skin conditions, not only what we now call leprosy. One bird is killed over fresh water and the living bird, dipped in its blood, is set free, probably picturing the person's own release, though the meaning of the cedar, red yarn and hyssop plant is uncertain.

parts.label: Washing, shaving and waiting (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: The person washes, shaves off all their hair and may come back into the camp, but must stay outside their own tent for seven days. On the seventh day they shave and wash again, so the return happens in stages rather than all at once.

parts.label: Offerings on the eighth day (vv. 10-20)
parts.note: At the entrance of the tent of meeting, the portable worship tent, the priest puts blood and then oil on the person's right ear, thumb and big toe, as was done when priests were first set apart in chapter 8. Many read this as restoring the whole person to worship, and the text says the priest makes atonement for them, a phrase whose exact sense in these purity rites scholars still debate.

parts.label: A cheaper way for the poor (vv. 21-32)
parts.note: Someone who cannot afford three lambs brings one lamb and two doves or pigeons instead. They go through the same ceremony and are declared just as fully clean.

parts.label: Mold in a house (vv. 33-47)
parts.note: Looking ahead to settled life in Canaan, this law treats spreading growth on walls, probably mold, mildew or a mineral crust, much like the skin disease. The house is emptied and shut for a week; if the growth has spread, the affected stones are replaced and the walls replastered, and only if it comes back after that is the house torn down.

parts.label: A house declared clean (vv. 48-57)
parts.note: If the growth does not return after the repair, the same two bird ceremony used for people marks the house clean. The closing lines wrap up chapters 13 and 14, whose stated purpose is to teach how to tell clean from unclean.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the details of these rites, such as the slain bird and the freed bird, were meant to point ahead to Jesus' death and resurrection, or are best read mainly as ancient Israel's way of marking a person's full return to community and worship.
think: When someone has been kept apart by illness or shame, what do you think it takes for a community to truly welcome them back?
